brief.topic: A Different Unit Can Change the Nearest Neighbor

s01: Can changing a unit change a machine learning prediction?
Here is a tiny nearest neighbor rule. It chooses the closest example.
The query is at zero. Example A is two steps right. Example B is three steps up.
Using these raw coordinates, the example on the right is closer.
Now write the first feature in units one hundred times smaller.
Two becomes two hundred. The second feature stays three.
Nothing about the examples has changed. Only our numerical ruler has changed.
But raw distance now chooses B.
Distance adds squared differences across features.
Before the conversion, the squared distances were four and nine.
Afterward, the first example gives forty thousand, compared with nine for the second.
The first feature has gained enormous influence just because of its unit.
We can choose a reference scale for each feature.
Divide each difference by its own reference scale before measuring distance.
Initially, let both scales be one.
When the first unit changes, its reference scale must change by the same factor.
Two hundred divided by one hundred is two again.
The dimensionless distances are back to two and three. Example A is closer again.
A consistent change of units now leaves the comparison unchanged.
The reference scales still matter. They express how differences should compare.
Learning useful scales from training data is one option, not a universal guarantee.
Before asking which example is nearest, ask what your ruler means.

scenes.narration:
Can changing a unit change a machine learning prediction? Here is a tiny nearest neighbor rule. It chooses the closest example. The query is at zero. Example A is two steps right. Example B is three steps up. Using these raw coordinates, the example on the right is closer.

Now write the first feature in units one hundred times smaller. Two becomes two hundred. The second feature stays three. Nothing about the examples has changed. Only our numerical ruler has changed. But raw distance now chooses B.

Distance adds squared differences across features. Before the conversion, the squared distances were four and nine. Afterward, the first example gives forty thousand, compared with nine for the second. The first feature has gained enormous influence just because of its unit.

We can choose a reference scale for each feature. Divide each difference by its own reference scale before measuring distance. Initially, let both scales be one. When the first unit changes, its reference scale must change by the same factor.

Two hundred divided by one hundred is two again. The dimensionless distances are back to two and three. Example A is closer again. A consistent change of units now leaves the comparison unchanged.

The reference scales still matter. They express how differences should compare. Learning useful scales from training data is one option, not a universal guarantee. Before asking which example is nearest, ask what your ruler means.
